claims.text: The proposed feedstock is high-purity, single-phase ZrB2 powder.
The intervention adds 3–5 wt% silicon to ZrB2 and uses spark plasma sintering at approximately 1700 °C.
Adding a few weight percent silicon enables ZrB2 to form a dense body by spark plasma sintering at approximately 1700 °C.
Silicon diffusion during sintering produces nanoscale silica-rich films along ZrB2 grain boundaries.
Silicon facilitates lower-temperature densification by enhancing mass transport during spark plasma sintering.
Residual silicon or in-situ-formed silica at grain boundaries acts as a protective barrier during high-temperature service.
The proposed grain-boundary barrier slows oxygen ingress.
The proposed grain-boundary barrier impedes liquid plating-metal penetration.
Silicon doping improves the oxidation resistance of ZrB2.
Silicon doping improves the liquid-metal corrosion resistance of ZrB2.
The oxidation and corrosion improvements can be achieved without compromising the inherent strength of ZrB2.
ZrB2 conventionally requires processing above 2300 °C for densification.
The silicon-doped material sintered at approximately 1700 °C will have densification comparable to single-phase ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C.
The silicon-doped material sintered at approximately 1700 °C will have mechanical integrity comparable to single-phase ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C.
The silicon-doped material will exhibit significantly better oxidation durability than conventional single-phase ZrB2.
The silicon-doped material will exhibit less corrosion in liquid plating-metal environments than conventional single-phase ZrB2.
The silicon-doped material will have better structural integrity and protective behavior than prior lower-temperature specimens.
Excessive silicon may produce undesirable second phases or adverse property trade-offs.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires densification comparable to the >2300 °C conventional control, whereas the falsification rule treats higher density than that control as evidence required for success. Thus, a result matching the stated prediction could nevertheless fail the stated falsification criterion.
